properties.title: EHR-MPC: Inference-Time Control for Sepsis Treatment with Generative Patient Digital Twins

properties.version_basis: PDF identified by SHA-256 against assignments.json; title page read.

properties.description: Inference-time model predictive control over a generative EHR digital twin for ICU sepsis treatment.
GPT-2-style token-level EHR digital twin with token-forced action rollouts, outcome heads and a receding-horizon MPC planner over four intervention options.

properties.algorithm: GPT-2-style decoder-only transformer over tokenized EHR events with task heads

properties.population: ICU patients with sepsis at eight hospitals of one health system
properties.user: clinician as human in the loop (stated aim)
properties.decision: vasopressor, antibiotic and corticosteroid treatment choice

capability_assessments.rationale: A simulation-based search over candidate action sequences chooses treatments and its policy value is evaluated by importance sampling and simulated outcomes, which meets L4. Evidence is retrospective and simulated, the twin has no identification guarantee and is confounded, there is no uncertainty, calibration or safety guard evidence, and the simulated advantage uses the same model family for planning and scoring.

Standalone generative digital twin model:B092:ehr-digital-twin:v1 implements tokenized persistent state, temporal autoregressive dynamics, and learned transformer transitions, and is evaluated on next-token/next-m forecasting (Table 3) and alternative-action dose-response counterfactual rollouts across steroids, vasopressors, and antibiotics from the same high-acuity patients (Table 4), meeting L3 without causal identification. Receding-horizon MPC policy search and WIS/simulated policy evaluation belong to the composed controller system:B092:ehr-mpc:v1 (L4), not the standalone dynamics model.

gate_assessments.rationale: A held-out set is mentioned (pp. 26-27), but train/validation/test split ratios, patient-level disjointness, and temporal split boundaries are not reported across pages 1-29.

Next-token and next-m set recall are reported with token-type stratification (Table 3, p. 11), but the train/test split design, patient-level disjointness, and non-leaky reference criteria are not specified across pages 1-29 (matching unresolved G01), preventing an evidence pass on G02.
No overlap or support analysis of candidate actions, and weighted importance sampling support issues are acknowledged.
A checkpoint-decoupling robustness test is reported, but planning and scoring models share data and architecture and no real-world outcome is observed.
Constraints are described as possible and no guard, abstention or monitoring is evaluated.

legacy_cells.B: EHR-MPC: Inference-Time Control for Sepsis Treatment with Generative Patient Digital Twins
legacy_cells.C: Pickard, Joshua, Qi, Wei, Li, Na, Woolley, Ann, Cosimi, Lisa, Kishony, Roy, et al.
legacy_cells.O: Sepsis in a cohort of ICU admissions that also included non-sepsis patients
legacy_cells.S: For an ICU sepsis patient’s current EHR history, which medication action sequence optimizes mortality risk or SOFA over the planning horizon?
legacy_cells.T: 36,930 ICU patients across eight hospitals, including 4,129 patients with sepsis; policy evaluation was restricted to sepsis patients.
legacy_cells.U: Clinicians (proposed clinical decision support; clinician feedback is contemplated).
legacy_cells.V: Select a vasopressor, antibiotic, or corticosteroid treatment action to optimize a specified mortality-risk or SOFA objective.
legacy_cells.X: F2 EHR / ICU event & latent patient dynamics
legacy_cells.AI: Tokenized longitudinal EHR events: vitals, laboratory measurements, medication/intervention events, procedures, device settings, diagnoses, demographics, and administrative events
legacy_cells.AJ: Decoder-only GPT-2-style causal language model / transformer; tokenized EHR input
legacy_cells.BD: Candidate medication actions are represented by drug tokens; four options include combinations of vasopressor, antibiotics, or steroids, or no administration of the specified medications; up to five representative drug tokens per drug class; simulated planning horizon is approximately 24 hours and policy actions are selected at daily intervals.
legacy_cells.BL: EHR stream includes four-hour interval tokens; MPC rollout generates six [4 hour] tokens, approximately 24 hours.
legacy_cells.BS: Autoregressively generated future EHR tokens representing patient-state trajectories, including clinical events, measurements, and interventions.
legacy_cells.BT: Mortality-risk prediction head and daily SOFA-delta prediction head; lightweight random-forest outcome readouts are also evaluated on learned representations.
legacy_cells.BU: Inference-time trajectory reward/objective minimizes predicted SOFA score or mortality risk.
legacy_cells.BV: Next-token prediction (NTP) for the EHR sequence; SOFA-delta head trained with mean squared error; mortality head trained with binary cross-entropy.
legacy_cells.CA: Base transformer trained on 7 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs for approximately 18 hours.
legacy_cells.CK: Optimize simulated trajectory reward for lower SOFA score or mortality risk; choose the candidate medication sequence with the highest predicted utility.
legacy_cells.DN: Mass General Brigham health-system institutional EHR database
legacy_cells.DQ: 36,930 ICU patients, including 4,129 patients with sepsis, with policy evaluation restricted to sepsis patients.
legacy_cells.DX: Next-m-token set recall: top-10 predictions, m=5 86.2% and m=10 82.8%; top-20, m=5 89.4% and m=10 85.9%; top-50, m=5 92.9% and m=10 89.9%. Token top-1/top-5/top-10 accuracy: medications 54.8%/74.0%/82.7%; location/unit 31.4%/58.7%/66.0%; labs, vitals, and orders 27.2%/54.3%/65.0%.
legacy_cells.EB: In 24-hour counterfactual rollouts with injected drug tokens, predicted mortality probabilities varied by drug and token count. Table 4 reports steroids 0.38 at 1 token and 0.12 at 20 tokens (with non-monotonic intermediate values); vasopressor and antibiotic responses also varied.
legacy_cells.EC: Off-policy WIS: EHR-MPC and Q-network had higher estimated value than the clinician policy, with similar EHR-MPC/Q-network point estimates and overlapping confidence intervals. In digital-twin simulations, EHR-MPC outperformed Q-network policies on daily SOFA improvement and mortality-risk reduction; advantage persisted under model-mismatch evaluation.
legacy_cells.EI: Q-network baseline: similar, overlapping off-policy WIS point estimates to EHR-MPC; lower simulation-based SOFA improvement and mortality-risk reduction. Clinician policy: lower WIS estimated value than EHR-MPC and Q-network.
legacy_cells.FL: Tokenized EHR events → ordered patient-history state x1:kt → GPT-2-style autoregressive transformer generating action-conditioned future EHR tokens → mortality-risk and SOFA-delta heads/trajectory reward → simulation-based MPC samples candidate medication sequences, scores rollouts, selects the first action, then repeats with updated patient state.
legacy_cells.FM: The authors propose EHR-MPC: learn generative patient dynamics separately from the clinical objective, then optimize medication treatment through inference-time MPC over simulated trajectories.
legacy_cells.FN: On the eight-hospital ICU cohort, EHR-MPC and Q-network had comparable WIS performance; EHR-MPC performed better in digital-twin simulation for SOFA improvement and mortality-risk reduction, including under model mismatch. The reported token forecast set recalls were 86.2%–92.9% at m=5 and 82.8%–89.9% at m=10 for top-10 through top-50 predictions.
legacy_cells.FO: The authors state that observational training is confounded by treatment indication and may yield hallucinated or unreliable trajectories for treatment regimes poorly represented in training data; twin fidelity and intervention validation lack guarantees. WIS has high variance and support-mismatch sensitivity, while simulator evaluation depends on model accuracy. They also note computational and hyperparameter optimization opportunities.
legacy_cells.FP: The authors identify improving digital-twin fidelity, prospectively validating learned dynamics, and developing principled evaluation frameworks for simulation-based policies as open problems for clinical translation.
legacy_cells.FQ: The authors argue that fixed-reward RL entangles patient dynamics with clinical objectives, limiting adaptation to changing goals; existing retrospective policy results are difficult to interpret, adapt, or validate clinically.
legacy_cells.FR: Evidence is retrospective and model-relative: WIS is observational/off-policy and high variance, while policy benefit is shown primarily in the learned simulator. Action-conditioned rollouts and dose-token sensitivity do not establish identified treatment effects; the authors acknowledge treatment-indication confounding and unreliable predictions for underrepresented regimens. No prospective clinical benefit or deployment is demonstrated.
legacy_cells.FS: Reviewer mapping: M3 Belief-state service; M4 Action service; M5 Dynamics adapter; M6 Rollout service; M7 Outcome & causal layer; M8 Planner; M9 Safety & governance
legacy_cells.FT: Reviewer lesson: Keep the learned patient/scene simulator separate from the planner objective; constrain candidate actions and report closed-loop decision quality alongside model fidelity.

legacy_cells.FZ: Full 29-page extracted text was readable. I did not browse or use external sources. A:I are omitted to preserve prefilled metadata; no direct contradiction requiring correction was identified. The evidence boundary is retrospective, multicenter, off-policy and model-relative simulation rather than prospective clinical benefit. The steroid dose-response table shows non-monotonic intermediate values despite the prose claim of a consistent monotonic decrease; EB reports the tabulated values without endorsing that claim. Blueprint module IDs and detailed open-problem taxonomy were referenced in the rubric but not defined in the supplied inputs, so FS is omitted and FU summarizes paper-supported open problems without assigning IDs. Evidence QA: 63/86 populated fields had a <=25-word quotation matching extracted PDF text (73.3%). Confidence is conservative; review this row where exact quote checks were incomplete. Codex audit: 80 prior populated fields have a located source quotation; 6 have quotations not located by normalized text matching. Unlocated quotations are review flags, not proof that the value is false. Companion evidence audit lists affected columns. Reviewer FS/FT/FU mappings are synthesis. Prior unsupported/missing fields remain Not reported; no clinical benefit inferred from offline simulation.

limitations: All 29 physical PDF pages were read as extracted text (including references pp. 17-22, Appendix A Tables 5-8 pp. 23-25, and Appendix B.6 Figures 6-8 p. 29). Rendered page images were visually inspected for pages 3 (Figure 1), 11-13 (Tables 3-4, Figures 2-3), 23-25 (Tables 5-8), and 29 (Figures 6-8).
Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 5, and Figures 6-8 plotted values were not digitized beyond printed annotations.
Train/validation/test split ratios, patient-level disjointness, and code/ethics/IRB approvals are not reported anywhere in the 29-page PDF; G01 and G02 remain unresolved.
The legacy row was read from the root workbook (read only). Saved API drafts for B092 were not opened.
Schema validity and quote occurrence do not establish semantic correctness. Automated repair review, no independent human review.
notes: EHR-MPC trains a GPT-2-style token-level EHR digital twin on 36,930 ICU patients from eight hospitals and plans over four intervention options by simulation-based search. Weighted importance sampling gives comparable value to a Q-network and simulations favor EHR-MPC, with a checkpoint-decoupling check. Forecasting recall is 82.8 to 92.9 percent for set recall and medication tokens are best predicted. The authors report non-monotonic responses for non-steroid drugs, and Table 4 steroid values are not monotonic although the text says they are. Classified L4, core, R2 (retrospective). Source points: confounding, no uncertainty or guard evidence, greedy decoding stated in the appendix.
